walkthroughs.body_html: The Amazon stores ~150-200 PgC in biomass and soils, equivalent to ~15-20 years of global anthropogenic emissions. Trees fix ~2 PgC/yr through photosynthesis. However, a 2021 Nature study (Gatti et al.) found the south-eastern Amazon is now a net carbon source due to deforestation and fires. Brazil's Amazon lost ~20% of its forest cover since 1970, ~13,000 km2 per year peaking in 2004.

The Amazon recycles ~50% of regional rainfall through evapotranspiration. Around 20 billion tonnes of water are released daily from forest canopies, more than the Amazon River discharges. These flying rivers water crops in southern Brazil, Argentina and Paraguay. Deforestation reduces transpiration, lengthens dry seasons, and risks savannisation: a tipping point estimated at 20-25% forest loss, after which the system flips irreversibly.

Deforestation drivers: cattle ranching (~80% of cleared land), soy (mainly for animal feed, with the 2006 Soy Moratorium reducing direct deforestation but driving indirect land conversion), illegal gold mining, and BR-163 and BR-319 highway expansion. Under Bolsonaro (2019-2022), deforestation rose 75% to ~13,000 km2/yr. Lula's 2023 government reduced rates by ~50% in one year through enforcement and IBAMA funding restoration.

mcqs.q: Why are tropical rainforest soils typically infertile?
options: Because rainforest soils are made of clay.
A tipping point is when world leaders agree to act on climate change.
Because so much vegetation grows there, the soil must be fertile.
Heavy rainfall leaches nutrients, and most nutrients are stored in living biomass and rapidly recycled — the soil itself holds very little.

mcqs.q: Why does the tropical rainforest have distinct vertical layers?
options: A tipping point is when world leaders agree to act on climate change.
Rainforest layers exist because trees grow in age order tallest to shortest.
Competition for light: emergents (40m+), canopy (capturing most light), understorey (shade-tolerant) and forest floor (sparse vegetation due to low light) — each adapted to its light level.
Rainforest layers exist because different animals live at different heights.

mcqs.q: What is a climate tipping point?
options: Because rainforest soils are made of clay.
A threshold beyond which a system changes irreversibly into a new state — e.g. the Amazon flipping from rainforest to savanna, or Greenland's ice sheet committing to total melt.
A tipping point is just when warming reaches 1.5 degrees C.
A tipping point is when world leaders agree to act on climate change.
